analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to disclose pricing methods and bars steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 56 cosponsors from both parties but never received a committee vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill sets rules for pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen that prescription drug plans hire to decide which drugs are covered, which pharmacies patients can use, and how much pharmacies get paid. Plans could not hire a PBM that sends a patient's prescription records to a pharmacy the PBM owns unless the patient chose that pharmacy, or that steers patients to PBM-owned pharmacies with incentives. Plans also would have had to update their pharmacy payment standards at least every 7 days to match what the drug actually costs, tell pharmacies where their pricing numbers come from, and resolve pharmacies' under-payment appeals within 7 days [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients whose prescription data would no longer flow to PBM-owned pharmacies without their consent; people enrolled in Medicare drug plans, Medicare Advantage, TRICARE, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits program; and community pharmacies, which would get current pricing information and a fast appeal when a plan pays them less than the drug cost them [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a PBM from transmitting a patient's identifiable prescription and claims data to a pharmacy the PBM owns unless the patient specifically chose that pharmacy for that prescription, and bars PBM-owned-pharmacy-only incentives to steer patients [S3].

Requires drug reimbursement standards used in Medicare Part D, Medicare Advantage, TRICARE retail pharmacy, and FEHB plans to be updated at least every 7 days to reflect the market price of acquiring the drug, with the pricing sources disclosed to pharmacies without a request [S3].

Gives pharmacies a dispute process, decided within 7 days, when a plan pays them below what the drug cost to acquire, and requires pricing data to be provided in a complete, easily accessible spreadsheet format [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies, which would lose the ability to route patients to their own pharmacies and would have to reveal and quickly update the formulas they use to pay pharmacies; plans and PBMs would also bear the administrative cost of weekly pricing updates and fast-tracked appeals [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies

drawbacks.text: The bill requires pricing transparency but does not directly cap what any patient pays for a drug, so a patient's out-of-pocket cost could stay the same even if pharmacies are paid more fairly [S2].
Reimbursing pharmacies closer to the real acquisition cost of drugs and shortening appeal timelines adds administrative work for plans and PBMs, a cost that could be passed on through premiums [S3].

Restricting PBM steering toward mail-order and specialty pharmacies they own removes one tool plans use to hold down drug spending, which an honest supporter would acknowledge could raise plan costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to patients is real but modest: stronger privacy over prescription data and less pressure to use a PBM-owned pharmacy, with any effect on what patients pay coming indirectly through pharmacy economics. The clearer gain goes to community pharmacies, which would finally see how their pay is set and get a quick appeal when a plan pays less than the drug costs. The costs fall on PBMs' profits and on some added plan administration — costs that do not fall on the public. On balance the bill is a fair, targeted fix, though limited in scope: it regulates the middlemen rather than drug prices themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then to subcommittees in March 2017, and it never advanced out of committee before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Doug Collins (R-GA) introduced the bill on March 2, 2017 with seven original cosponsors from both parties [S1].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees on the day it was introduced [S5].
By mid-April 2017 it had been referred to subcommittees on Health (twice, reflecting the split committee referrals) and Military Personnel [S5].
The bill finished the Congress with 56 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 42 Republicans, but no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action after the subcommittee referrals [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest pharmacy benefit managers kept their existing practices: opaque pharmacy payment formulas, the ability to steer patients to pharmacies they own, and access to patient prescription data without consent. The PBM industry's position was untouched when the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 42 Republicans and 14 Democrats, and there were no votes on the bill at any stage; the only recorded action, referral to four committees, was unanimous.

industries.note: The bill bars PBMs from steering patients to pharmacies they own and from receiving patient prescription data without consent, and forces them to disclose and weekly-update the formulas used to pay pharmacies. PBMs profit from opaque payment formulas and routing volume to their own mail-order and specialty pharmacies, so their business interest runs against the patients and pharmacies this bill protects.

Pharmacies would learn the sources behind their reimbursement rates within days instead of never, get paid rates updated weekly to match actual acquisition cost, and resolve under-payment appeals within 7 days. Their gain on reimbursement flows directly into patients' access to local pharmacies.

industries.industry: Prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Insurers would have to enforce the new PBM standards and update their own pricing standards weekly, adding administration, but they also gain a clearer, fairer contract framework with their PBM vendors.
